traps.trap: Haemorrhage is the leading preventable death, so control bleeding before securing the airway (also absorbs TR13: xABCDE / MARCH order carried into an ATLS question)

probes.stem_idea: Trauma patient with a bleeding limb wound arrives; what is the first priority in the ATLS primary survey?
probes.correct: Airway with restriction of cervical spine motion
distractor_set: Control of external haemorrhage with a tourniquet [TR1]
Two large-bore IV lines with crystalloid [TR1]
Rapid neurological assessment with GCS [partial: correct-adjacent step, wrong position]
probes.note: Keep all four options the same length and grammar. The trap is picking the visible, dramatic problem.

probes.stem_idea: A military medic uses catastrophic haemorrhage first. For an ATLS-based exam question, which is the expected primary-survey order?
probes.correct: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure
probes.note: Teach both: prehospital protocols (K133, shown with warning, unverified) put bleeding first; ATLS keeps haemorrhage control inside C.

probes.stem_idea: Unresponsive patient, snoring respirations, pelvis tender, blood on the trousers; which action comes first and why?
probes.correct: Jaw thrust with suction to open the airway
distractor_set: Pelvic binder to stop the blood loss [TR1]
Log-roll and examine the back [partial: secondary-survey habit]
probes.note: Re-test with a snoring airway sign that makes A unmistakable; a bleeding source is present as bait.

traps.diagnoses: Learner ranks problems by how visible or how common a killer they are, not by how fast each one kills.
traps.first_wrong_step: Reads 'most common preventable death' as 'first to treat', mixing frequency with speed of killing.

repair.strategy: E9: order the steps by time-to-death (airway minutes, breathing minutes, blood longer) and ask 'what first, and why'; then teach the MARCH conflict as a both-sides note

traps.retest: Third probe in a vignette with a snoring airway; again in the consolidation sequence-building step.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they order by speed of death. Fell and recovered: they now separate frequency from priority. Fell and stayed fallen: they still put the loudest problem first; tell them to ask 'what kills in minutes' before 'what bleeds most'.

traps.trap: A patient who talks is fully safe, so the primary survey can stop there

probes.stem_idea: A man with a chest wound answers questions clearly at the door; what is the next step in the primary survey?
probes.correct: Assess breathing and ventilation
distractor_set: Check disability, since talking shows breathing and circulation are fine [TR2]
Intubate to protect the airway [partial: unneeded step for a talking patient]
probes.note: Trap is stretching 'talking' beyond 'for the moment, airway'. Two options map to TR2 on purpose: skip-ahead and over-extend.

probes.stem_idea: The same patient, a few minutes later, becomes hoarse with an expanding neck swelling; what does this show?
probes.correct: Airway status can change, so reassess A repeatedly
distractor_set: Earlier speech proved the airway safe, so this is unrelated [TR2]
Hoarseness is expected and needs only analgesia [partial]
A definitive airway is already required for any trauma patient [partial]
probes.note: Re-tests the qualifier 'for the moment' with the airway deteriorating.

traps.diagnoses: Learner treats a reassuring sign as a permanent all-clear, dropping the 'for the moment' qualifier.
traps.first_wrong_step: Converts 'patent now' into 'safe throughout' and stops reassessing.

repair.strategy: E4: show the exact qualifier in the claim and give a counter-case where the airway fails after the patient spoke

traps.retest: Second probe with a deteriorating airway; recurs in the cold last-segment vignette.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they hear 'for the moment'. Recovered: they now reassess. Stayed fallen: they treat one good sign as an all-clear; advise repeating ABCDE with every change.

traps.trap: Tension pneumothorax needs a chest X-ray before decompression

probes.stem_idea: Hypotensive, distended neck veins, hyper-resonant right chest, absent breath sounds on the right; what is the next step?
probes.correct: Immediate needle decompression of the right chest
probes.note: Probe also surfaces TR5 and TR8 in the same stem; each option maps to one trap.

probes.stem_idea: How is tension pneumothorax diagnosed?
probes.correct: Clinically, at the bedside
probes.note: Distractors are plausible 'confirm first' tests; the key is the shortest only if padded, so match lengths.

traps.diagnoses: Learner applies the usual 'image then treat' routine to a condition that kills before an image can be taken.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats the investigation ladder as fixed, without asking whether the patient can afford the delay.

repair.strategy: E8: ladder of tests with what each answers; place 'clinical diagnosis' as the top rung when shock is present

traps.retest: Second probe as recognition; reappears in the thoracic look-alike contrast and the final cold vignette.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they decompress on clinical grounds. Recovered: they now accept bedside diagnosis. Stayed fallen: they still wait for imaging in a collapsing patient.

traps.trap: An unstable trauma patient goes to CT for abdominal bleeding (also absorbs TR24: FAST treated as confirming organ injury)

probes.stem_idea: Blunt abdominal trauma, hypotensive and not responding to fluid; what is the best initial test?
probes.correct: Bedside FAST in the resuscitation room
probes.note: CT is the most sensitive test, which is why it tempts; the key is the qualifier unstable.

probes.stem_idea: A positive FAST in a stable patient: what does it show and what is the next test?
probes.correct: Free fluid only; CT defines the organ injury
distractor_set: It confirms the splenic laceration, so no further imaging is needed [TR4]
Free fluid only; repeat FAST every hour instead [partial]
probes.note: Same ladder, reversed direction: screening versus defining test.

traps.diagnoses: Learner picks the most sensitive test without checking whether the patient is stable enough to travel, and treats a screening test as a confirmatory one.
traps.first_wrong_step: Chooses by test accuracy rather than by patient stability.

repair.strategy: E8: ladder of tests: unstable gets FAST or DPL in the room, stable gets CT; say what each rung answers

traps.retest: Second probe in a stable patient so the same ladder is read upward; final-segment vignette.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they pick by stability. Recovered: they now stratify tests by stability. Stayed fallen: they equate best test with first test.

traps.trap: Ventilate or intubate the tension pneumothorax patient before decompressing

probes.stem_idea: Talking patient with a patent airway, desaturating, hypotensive, absent breath sounds on one side; what is done first?
probes.correct: Needle decompression of the affected side
distractor_set: Supplemental oxygen by mask and re-examine in 10 minutes [partial]
probes.note: Airway is patent, which removes the reason to reach for the tube. Trap is 'A comes first, so tube'.

probes.stem_idea: Why does positive-pressure ventilation worsen an untreated tension pneumothorax?
probes.correct: It pushes more air into a trapped space, raising pressure and impeding venous return
distractor_set: It re-expands the collapsed lung and relieves the shift [TR5]
It collapses the opposite lung by overinflation [partial]
It only matters if the patient is awake [partial]
probes.note: Predict-then-show structure: learner predicts the effect of positive pressure.

traps.diagnoses: Learner reaches for the intubation because the airway is the first letter, ignoring that positive pressure feeds the leak.
traps.first_wrong_step: Fixes hypoxia with positive pressure without noticing a one-way valve is the cause.

repair.strategy: E9 with E3 flavour: trace the one-way valve step by step, then order: decompress first, then airway

traps.retest: Second probe as mechanism; recurs as a 'what next after needle decompression' step in the management segment.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they treat the cause. Recovered: they decompress before ventilating. Stayed fallen: they follow letters mechanically rather than physiology.

traps.trap: Hypotension with bradycardia in trauma is haemorrhagic shock

probes.stem_idea: Fall from height, paraplegia, low BP with a slow pulse and warm dry extremities; which shock?
probes.correct: Neurogenic shock
probes.note: The caveat in K7 (hypovolaemia until proven otherwise) is the reason the trap tempts; the slow pulse and warm skin discriminate.

probes.stem_idea: Which finding best separates neurogenic from haemorrhagic shock?
probes.correct: Slow heart rate with warm peripheries
probes.note: Distractors are findings shared by both shock types, so choosing them shows the look-alike model.

traps.diagnoses: Learner anchors on 'trauma plus low BP means bleeding' and ignores the heart rate and skin that separate the two shocks.
traps.first_wrong_step: Stops at hypotension and does not read the pulse.

repair.strategy: E1: side-by-side contrast of neurogenic and haemorrhagic shock with the discriminating feature

traps.retest: Second probe in contrast form; recurs among obstructive-shock options in the thoracic segment.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they read the pulse. Recovered: they now use rate and skin to separate shocks. Stayed fallen: they equate low BP with blood loss.

traps.trap: Tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax look the same on examination

probes.stem_idea: Shock, absent breath sounds on one side, dull percussion, flat neck veins; what is the diagnosis?
probes.correct: Massive haemothorax
probes.note: Percussion and neck veins carry the answer; absent breath sounds is the shared decoy.

probes.stem_idea: Which finding best distinguishes tension pneumothorax from massive haemothorax?
probes.correct: Hyper-resonance with distended neck veins
distractor_set: Absent breath sounds on the affected side [TR7]
probes.note: Each distractor is true of both conditions.

probes.stem_idea: Stab wound to the chest, hyper-resonant hemithorax, trachea shifted, distended neck veins; what does the patient need?
probes.correct: Needle decompression, then a chest tube
distractor_set: Chest tube after a chest X-ray [TR3]
Chest tube with rapid blood replacement as for haemothorax [TR7]
probes.note: Reverse direction: a learner who thinks they look alike will manage as haemothorax.

traps.diagnoses: Learner stops at 'shock with absent breath sounds' and never uses percussion or neck veins to separate air from blood.
traps.first_wrong_step: Takes the shared finding as the discriminator.

repair.strategy: E1: contrasting cases, air versus blood, naming percussion and neck veins as the discriminators

traps.retest: Second and third probes use contrast and a reversed vignette.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they percuss and read the veins. Recovered: they now separate air from blood. Stayed fallen: they treat any unilateral silent chest as one problem.

traps.trap: Beck's triad belongs to tension pneumothorax

probes.stem_idea: Stab wound near the left parasternal region, hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, clear breath sounds; what is the diagnosis?
probes.correct: Cardiac tamponade
probes.note: Breath sounds are clear, which is the discriminator against tension pneumothorax.

probes.stem_idea: Beck's triad consists of which findings?
probes.correct: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins
probes.note: Each distractor is the triad of another shock; the whole set is a one-trap-per-option contrast.

traps.diagnoses: Learner merges two obstructive causes because both give hypotension and distended neck veins.
traps.first_wrong_step: Takes hypotension plus raised neck veins as sufficient and ignores heart sounds and breath sounds.

repair.strategy: E1: side-by-side table of tamponade versus tension pneumothorax with heart sounds, breath sounds and percussion

traps.retest: Second probe as recognition; the list retest TR35 also touches tamponade.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they check heart and breath sounds. Recovered: they now keep the two obstructive shocks apart. Stayed fallen: they stop at raised neck veins.

traps.trap: Hypotension appears early in haemorrhage (Class II)

probes.stem_idea: In haemorrhagic shock, in which class does hypotension first appear?
probes.correct: Class III, with 31 to 40 percent blood loss
distractor_set: Class II, with 15 to 30 percent blood loss [TR9]
Class I, with up to 15 percent blood loss [TR9]
Class IV, with more than 40 percent blood loss [partial]
probes.note: Keep each option as class plus range so none stands out by form.

probes.stem_idea: 70-kg adult with about a quarter of blood volume lost, pulse raised, BP normal, narrowed pulse pressure; which class, and why is BP normal?
probes.correct: Class II, compensated; narrowed pulse pressure appears first
distractor_set: Class II, already decompensated with falling systolic BP [TR9]
Class I, since BP is normal [partial]
Class III, with hypotension masked by anxiety [partial]
probes.note: Re-tests the number in an applied form; the early sign is narrowed pulse pressure and tachycardia.

traps.diagnoses: Learner assumes shock signs and blood-loss percentage rise in step, so that low BP shows up as soon as loss is moderate.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not account for compensation that holds the systolic BP until a third of volume is gone.

repair.strategy: E6: anchor the number to compensation (BP holds until about a third of blood is gone); retest in vignette form

traps.retest: Second probe as a vignette; recurs in the special-population segment with TR17.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they know BP is a late sign. Recovered: they anchor to compensation. Stayed fallen: they wait for low BP before acting.

traps.trap: Initial crystalloid bolus is 2 L in adults (old PYQ key; Ringer-lactate-only variant TR12 handled in feedback)

probes.stem_idea: ATLS 10th edition: initial fluid bolus in an adult?
probes.correct: 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid
distractor_set: 20 mL/kg warmed isotonic crystalloid [partial: child dose]
probes.note: Teach both: older keys expected 2 L; ATLS 10th edition says 1 L and early blood. K130 can note that RL and saline are both accepted.

probes.stem_idea: Why did ATLS reduce the initial crystalloid volume and bring blood products in early?
probes.correct: Large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors, cool the patient and worsen bleeding
distractor_set: Two litres is the paediatric bolus and too much for adults [TR10]
Crystalloids are toxic in haemorrhagic shock [partial]
Adult blood volume is lower than first thought [partial]
probes.note: Mechanism anchors the new number so it survives the PYQ pull.

traps.diagnoses: Learner answers with the number printed in older books and keys without checking the edition the question follows.
traps.first_wrong_step: Retrieves the familiar figure rather than asking which edition or key is in force.

repair.strategy: E5: teach both, 'PYQs expected 2 L; ATLS 10th edition says 1 L', then give the reason for the change

traps.retest: Second probe as mechanism; recurs in the consolidation numbers set.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they know both keys. Recovered: they can state the old and the new figure. Stayed fallen: they will lose marks on any question that follows the current edition.

traps.trap: Needle decompression goes in the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, in adults

probes.stem_idea: ATLS 10th edition: site of needle decompression in an adult?
probes.correct: 4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line
probes.note: Teach both: PYQs and older texts expect 2nd ICS MCL; ATLS 10th edition moved the adult site.

probes.stem_idea: Needle decompression in a 6-year-old with tension pneumothorax; where?
probes.correct: 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
distractor_set: 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line [partial: adult site, qualifier ignored]
5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line, as for a chest tube [partial]
probes.note: The old site is still right for children, so the old key is not wholly wrong; this blocks over-correction.

traps.diagnoses: Learner holds the older memorised site and does not tie site to age or to the edition in force.
traps.first_wrong_step: Retrieves the site that was the standard answer in older books.

repair.strategy: E5: both keys side by side, then the reason (catheter too short at the 2nd ICS in a thick chest wall) and the child exception

traps.retest: Second probe in a paediatric form; recurs in the final management vignette.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they give adult and child sites. Recovered: they hold both keys. Stayed fallen: they will answer the old site; note both versions before the exam.

traps.trap: Paradoxical chest-wall movement causes the hypoxia in flail chest

probes.stem_idea: What is the main cause of hypoxia in flail chest?
probes.correct: Underlying pulmonary contusion
distractor_set: Paradoxical movement of the flail segment [TR14]
probes.note: The paradoxical segment is the visible sign; the contusion is the cause.

probes.stem_idea: Flail chest with hypoxia; which management addresses the cause?
probes.correct: Oxygen, analgesia and cautious fluids
distractor_set: Urgent surgical stabilisation of the segment [TR14]
Aggressive crystalloid to flush the lung [partial]
probes.note: Wrong options all treat the movement rather than the contusion.

traps.diagnoses: Learner mistakes the visible sign for the cause of the physiological problem.
traps.first_wrong_step: Assumes the sign that defines the injury also explains the hypoxia.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show; ask what would happen if the segment were stabilised but the lung stayed bruised, then trace the contusion

traps.retest: Second probe as a management vignette; also appears in the TR35 list.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they link hypoxia to contusion. Recovered: they separate sign from cause. Stayed fallen: they treat the movement, not the lung.

traps.trap: Tracheal deviation points toward the injured side in tension pneumothorax

probes.stem_idea: Right-sided tension pneumothorax: which pair of findings is expected?
probes.correct: Trachea deviated to the left with hyper-resonance on the right
distractor_set: Trachea deviated to the right with hyper-resonance on the right [TR16]
Trachea central with dullness on the right [TR7]
Trachea deviated to the right with dullness on the right [partial]
probes.note: Option lengths and structure match; direction is the only difference between key and trap.

probes.stem_idea: As pressure builds in the pleural space, what happens to the mediastinum?
probes.correct: It is pushed to the opposite side, kinking the great veins
distractor_set: It is pulled toward the collapsed lung [TR16]
It stays midline while the lung collapses [partial]
It shifts only after the diaphragm flattens [partial]
probes.note: Predict-then-show: learner predicts direction before the explanation.

traps.diagnoses: Learner reverses the direction of mediastinal shift, picturing a collapsed lung pulling things toward it.
traps.first_wrong_step: Imagines the collapse as the force instead of the trapped air under pressure.

repair.strategy: E3: predict then show; trace one-way valve, rising pressure, push to the opposite side, venous return falls

traps.retest: Second probe as mechanism; recurs in the thoracic contrast step.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they know pressure pushes. Recovered: direction now correct. Stayed fallen: they still picture collapse pulling the trachea.

traps.trap: Normal vital signs exclude shock in children, the elderly, pregnancy and beta-blocked patients

probes.stem_idea: 70-year-old on a beta-blocker after a fall: heart rate and BP normal, pale and cool skin; how do you read this?
probes.correct: Shock may be present; the usual compensatory signs are blunted
distractor_set: No shock, since vital signs are normal [TR17]
Class I haemorrhage, since vital signs are normal [TR9]
Neurogenic shock, because the pulse is not fast [TR6]
probes.note: Qualifiers in the stem are age and drug; learners who drop them choose the first option.

probes.stem_idea: A 10-year-old after a road traffic accident: cool, mottled, fast pulse, BP normal; what next?
probes.correct: Treat as compensated shock; hypotension will be a late sign
distractor_set: Wait for hypotension before giving fluid [TR17]
probes.note: Same trap, different qualifier (age). A pregnancy vignette can serve as a third surface in the consolidate segment.

traps.diagnoses: Learner uses normal vitals as default reassurance and drops the qualifiers that blunt them.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not check whether this patient could have a blunted heart rate or BP response.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier; contrast two patients with identical vitals, one healthy adult and one qualifier patient

traps.retest: Second probe changes the qualifier from age and drug to child; consolidation adds pregnancy.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they check the qualifier first. Recovered: they now doubt normal vitals in special groups. Stayed fallen: they trust normal vitals; check age, pregnancy and drugs every time.

traps.trap: Surgical cricothyroidotomy is the emergency airway for a child

probes.stem_idea: An 8-year-old with facial burns, cannot intubate and cannot oxygenate; what is the emergency airway?
probes.correct: Needle cricothyroidotomy
probes.note: The adult answer fits the vignette except for age, so the qualifier is the whole trap.

probes.stem_idea: Same failed-airway situation in a 35-year-old and a 9-year-old: which pair of surgical airways?
probes.correct: Surgical cricothyroidotomy; needle cricothyroidotomy
probes.note: Pair contrast so the learner states both halves of the rule.

traps.diagnoses: Learner holds the adult answer and drops the age qualifier.
traps.first_wrong_step: Reads 'surgical airway' and retrieves the adult rule without checking age.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier; explain the cricoid as the only complete ring, then contrast adult with child

traps.retest: Second probe contrasts adult and child; final cold vignette reuses an age cue.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they check age. Recovered: they now split adult and child. Stayed fallen: they apply adult rules to a child.

traps.trap: Insert a urinary catheter first to check for urethral injury

probes.stem_idea: Pelvic fracture with blood at the meatus and a high-riding prostate; what comes before a catheter?
probes.correct: Retrograde urethrogram
distractor_set: Foley catheter to measure urine output [TR23]
probes.note: The catheter is routine in primary survey; the injury sign is the qualifier.

probes.stem_idea: In a pelvic trauma patient with suspected urethral injury, when is a urinary catheter placed?
probes.correct: After a urethrogram shows an intact urethra
distractor_set: Before anything else, to monitor output [TR23]
After the pelvic X-ray alone looks reassuring [partial]
probes.note: Sequence form re-tests the same rule.

traps.diagnoses: Learner follows the routine of early catheter placement and misses the signs that forbid it.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats the catheter as automatic and does not scan for meatal blood or a high prostate.

repair.strategy: E8: ladder of tests with what each answers; the urethrogram answers 'is the urethra intact', which must precede the catheter

traps.retest: Second probe as a sequence; recurs in the final vignette with a pelvic injury.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they look for meatal blood. Recovered: urethrogram before catheter. Stayed fallen: they still catheterise by habit.

traps.trap: The third peak (sepsis, days to weeks) is the window ATLS targets

probes.stem_idea: Which peak of the trimodal distribution does ATLS target?
probes.correct: Second peak, minutes to hours after injury
distractor_set: Third peak, days to weeks after injury [TR30]
First peak, seconds to minutes after injury [partial]
probes.note: Mild PYQ-vs-current note (K21, K131 unverified) can be shown with a warning.

probes.stem_idea: Which of these deaths belongs to the second peak?
probes.correct: Ruptured spleen with bleeding 2 hours after a crash
distractor_set: High cervical cord transection at the scene [partial]
probes.note: The trap option is a late death that learners link to training.

traps.diagnoses: Learner links the commonest late complication with the course and misplaces the target window.
traps.first_wrong_step: Picks the most familiar cause of death rather than the one that early resuscitation can change.

repair.strategy: E10: pair each peak with its examples and what can change it (prevention, resuscitation, ICU care)

traps.retest: Second probe as examples-to-peak matching.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they pair peaks with what changes them. Recovered: they now match ATLS to the second peak. Stayed fallen: they link ATLS to sepsis.

traps.trap: A chest injury list for the primary survey is any chest injury, including simple pneumothorax and rib fractures, with tamponade left out

probes.stem_idea: Which is NOT one of the life-threatening chest injuries identified in the primary survey?
probes.correct: Simple closed pneumothorax
probes.note: Distractors are true set members; a learner who drops a member (often tamponade) picks one.

probes.stem_idea: Which of these chest injuries is assessed with circulation rather than breathing?
probes.correct: Cardiac tamponade
probes.note: Set logic: five life-threatening injuries, four under B and tamponade under C.

traps.diagnoses: Learner has not stored the life-threatening chest injuries as a set with its own logic.
traps.first_wrong_step: Adds any serious-looking chest injury to the list and drops tamponade because it is a heart problem.

repair.strategy: E2: rebuild the set from its logic (threat to oxygenation, ventilation, or filling) and retest with which-is-NOT

traps.retest: Second probe in a different form; consolidation card for the five.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they hold the five. Recovered: set rebuilt from logic. Stayed fallen: they learn chest injuries as a vague pile; rebuild the set.

traps.trap: Permissive hypotension is the target in traumatic brain injury

probes.stem_idea: Pelvic fracture bleeding with a head injury and low GCS; what is the blood pressure target?
probes.correct: Maintain adequate perfusion pressure for the brain
distractor_set: Accept a low BP to avoid popping the clot [TR18]
Withhold fluids until the operating theatre [TR18]
probes.note: Permissive hypotension is high-yield for haemorrhage; the TBI exception is the qualifier.

probes.stem_idea: In which patient is permissive hypotension acceptable until bleeding is controlled?
probes.correct: Penetrating torso injury with no head injury
distractor_set: Haemorrhagic shock with traumatic brain injury [TR18]
probes.note: Positive version of the exception.

traps.diagnoses: Learner applies a high-yield haemorrhage rule without checking for a coexisting brain injury.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not ask whether the brain needs a higher perfusion pressure.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier; contrast haemorrhage alone with haemorrhage plus brain injury

traps.retest: Second probe as a contrast of patients.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they check for head injury. Recovered: exception learnt. Stayed fallen: permissive hypotension applied to everyone.

traps.trap: Tranexamic acid works up to 8 hours

probes.stem_idea: Tranexamic acid in bleeding trauma should be started within what time of injury?
probes.correct: 3 hours
probes.note: The 8-hour figure is the maintenance infusion; options kept the same form.

probes.stem_idea: A bleeding patient arrives 5 hours after injury; is TXA indicated and what is the regimen when it is?
probes.correct: Outside the 3-hour window; regimen is 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours when inside it
distractor_set: Yes, give 1 g over 8 hours only [TR27]
probes.note: Apply the window and separate it from the infusion duration; shorten the key wording when authoring so it is not the longest.

traps.diagnoses: Learner confuses the infusion duration with the treatment window.
traps.first_wrong_step: Picks the most memorable TXA number and files it under the wrong label.

repair.strategy: E6: anchor the numbers (3 hours is the window, 8 hours is the infusion) and retest in a vignette

traps.retest: Second probe as a vignette; consolidation number set.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: they separate window and infusion. Recovered: numbers relabelled. Stayed fallen: they will give TXA late.

dropped.reason: merged into TR10 (same E5 fluid-key conflict; RL versus saline handled in TR10 feedback via K125, K130)
merged into TR1 (same C-before-A confusion; MARCH versus ATLS as the both-keys note, K133 unverified)
merged into TR4 (FAST screening versus defining test, second probe)
medium yield; head injury versus hypotension covered by TR6 and K30 feedback
medium yield; covered inside TR22 distractors
medium yield number trap; cap of 20 traps (TR9 and TR27 carry E6)
low yield, and refuted only by unverified claims
medium yield; sequence idea covered by TR1
medium yield; look-alike partly covered as a distractor in TR22

probe_plan: Backbone traps, in the order met: TR1 (priority by speed of death), TR2 (talking is only 'for now'), TR5 and TR3 (tension pneumothorax is treated first and clinically; they share one vignette), TR7 with TR16 and TR8 (the thoracic look-alike cluster, taught by contrast; TR7 is the hub), TR6 (shock types), TR9 with TR17 (compensation hides hypotension; TR17 reuses the number), and TR4 (unstable goes to FAST). Order: TR1, TR2 in the opening hook and ABCDE segment; TR3, TR5, TR16, TR7, TR8, TR35, TR14 in the breathing and chest segment (TR3 first because TR5, TR7 and TR8 offer it as a distractor in the same stems); TR6, TR9, TR17, TR4, TR23 and TR10, TR18, TR27 in the circulation and fluid segment; TR11 and TR22 in management; TR30 early as a bridge or in the consolidate segment. TR3, TR5, TR7, TR8 and TR6 are cross-offered as distractors, so a vignette stem can test several traps at once, with one trap per option. Every trap has at least two probes in different forms; TR1 and TR7 have three because they feed the most later stems. TR10, TR11, TR1, TR27 and TR30 carry PYQ-key or old-edition conflicts and need a teach-both repair before the re-test.
